comes with a full [Postgres](https://www.postgresql.org/) database, a free and open source database which is considered one of the world's most stable and advanced databases.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Features\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Table view\\\\n\\\\nYou don't have to be a database expert to start using Supabase. Our table view makes Postgres as easy to use as a spreadsheet.\\\\n\\\\n![Table View.](/docs/img/table-view.png)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Relationships\\\\n\\\\nDig into the relationships within your data.\\\\n\\\\n<video width=\\\\\\\"99%\\\\\\\" loop muted playsInline controls={true}>\\\\n  <source src=\\\\\\\"https://xguihxuzqibwxjnimxev.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/videos/docs/relational-drilldown-zoom.mp4\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"video/mp4\\\\\\\" />\\\\n</video>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Clone tables\\\\n\\\\nYou can duplicate your tables, just like you would inside a spreadsheet.\\\\n\\\\n<video width=\\\\\\\"99%\\\\\\\" muted playsInline controls={true}>\\\\n  <source src=\\\\\\\"https://xguihxuzqibwxjnimxev.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/videos/docs/duplicate-tables.mp4\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"video/mp4\\\\\\\" />\\\\n</video>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### The SQL editor\\\\n\\\\nSupabase comes with a SQL Editor. You can also save your favorite queries to run later!\\\\n\\\\n<video width=\\\\\\\"99%\\\\\\\" muted playsInline controls={true}>\\\\n  <source src=\\\\\\\"https://xguihxuzqibwxjnimxev.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/videos/docs/favorites.mp4\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"video/mp4\\\\\\\" />\\\\n</video>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Additional features\\\\n\\\\n*   Supabase extends Postgres with realtime functionality using our [Realtime Server](https://github.com/supabase/realtime).\\\\n*   Every project is a full Postgres database, with `postgres` level access.\\\\n*   Supabase manages your database backups.\\\\n*   Import data directly from a CSV or excel spreadsheet.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Database backups **do not** include objects stored via the Storage API, as the database only includes metadata about these objects. Restoring an old backup does not restore objects that have been deleted since then.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Extensions\\\\n\\\\nTo expand the functionality of your Postgres database, you can use extensions.\\\\nYou can enable Postgres extensions with the click of a button within the Supabase dashboard.\\\\n\\\\n<video width=\\\\\\\"99%\\\\\\\" muted playsInline controls={true}>\\\\n  <source src=\\\\\\\"https://xguihxuzqibwxjnimxev.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/videos/docs/toggle-extensions.mp4\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"video/mp4\\\\\\\" />\\\\n</video>\\\\n\\\\n[Learn more](/docs/guides/database/extensions) about all the extensions provided on Supabase.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Terminology\\\\n\\\\n{/* supa-mdx-lint-disable-next-line Rule004ExcludeWords */}\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Postgres or PostgreSQL?\\\\n\\\\n{/* supa-mdx-lint-disable-next-line Rule004ExcludeWords */}\\\\n\\\\nPostgreSQL the database was derived from the POSTGRES Project, a package written at the University of California at Berkeley in 1986. This package included a query language called \\\\\\\"PostQUEL\\\\\\\".\\\\n\\\\nIn 1994, Postgres95 was built on top of POSTGRES code, adding an SQL language interpreter as a replacement for PostQUEL.\\\\n\\\\n{/* supa-mdx-lint-disable-next-line Rule004ExcludeWords */}\\\\n\\\\nEventually, Postgres95 was renamed to PostgreSQL to reflect the SQL query capability.\\\\nAfter this, many people referred to it as Postgres since it's less prone to confusion. Supabase is all about simplicity, so we also refer to it as Postgres.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Tips\\\\n\\\\nRead about resetting your database password [here](/docs/guides/database/managing-passwords) and changing the timezone of your server [here](/docs/guides/database/managing-timezones).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Next steps\\\\n\\\\n*   Read more about [Postgres](https://www.postgresql.org/about/)\\\\n*   Sign in: [supabase.com/dashboard](/dashboard)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"OrioleDB Overview\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/orioledb\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# OrioleDB Overview\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nThe [OrioleDB](https://www.orioledb.com/) Postgres extension provides a drop-in replacement storage engine for the default heap storage method. It is designed to improve Postgres' scalability and performance.\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB addresses PostgreSQL's scalability limitations by removing bottlenecks in the shared memory cache under high concurrency. It also optimizes write-ahead-log (WAL) insertion through row-level WAL logging. These changes lead to significant improvements in the industry standard TPC-C benchmark, which approximates a real-world transactional workload. The following benchmark was performed on a c7g.metal instance and shows OrioleDB's performance outperforming the default Postgres heap method with a 3.3x speedup.\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"TPC-C (warehouses = 500)\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/orioledb-tpc-c-500-warehouse.png\\\\\\\" className=\\\\\\\"max-w-[550px] !mx-auto border rounded-md\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  OrioleDB is in active development and currently has [certain limitations](https://www.orioledb.com/docs/usage/getting-started#current-limitations). Currently, only B-tree indexes are supported, so features like pg\\\\\\\\_vector's HNSW indexes are not yet available. An Index Access Method bridge to unlock support for all index types used with heap storage is under active development. In the Supabase OrioleDB image the default storage method has been updated to use OrioleDB, granting better performance out of the box.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Concepts\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Index-organized tables\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB uses index-organized tables, where table data is stored in the index structure. This design eliminates the need for separate heap storage, reduces overhead and improves lookup performance for primary key queries.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### No buffer mapping\\\\n\\\\nIn-memory pages are connected to the storage pages using direct links. This allows OrioleDB to bypass PostgreSQL's shared buffer pool and eliminate the associated complexity and contention in buffer mapping.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Undo log\\\\n\\\\nMulti-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) is implemented using an undo log. The undo log stores previous row versions and transaction information, which enables consistent reads while removing the need for table vacuuming completely.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Copy-on-write checkpoints\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB implements copy-on-write checkpoints to persist data efficiently. This approach writes only modified data during a checkpoint, reducing the I/O overhead compared to traditional Postgres checkpointing and allowing row-level WAL logging.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Usage\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating OrioleDB project\\\\n\\\\nYou can get started with OrioleDB by enabling the extension in your Supabase dashboard.\\\\nTo get started with OrioleDB you need to [create a new Supabase project](/dashboard/new/_) and choose `OrioleDB Public Alpha` Postgres version.\\\\n\\\\n<Image\\\\n  alt=\\\\\\\"Creating OrioleDB project\\\\\\\"\\\\n  src={{\\\\n    light: '/docs/img/database/orioledb-creating-project--light.png',\\\\n    dark: '/docs/img/database/orioledb-creating-project.png',\\\\n  }}\\\\n  className=\\\\\\\"max-w-[550px] !mx-auto border rounded-md\\\\\\\"\\\\n  zoomable\\\\n/>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating tables\\\\n\\\\nTo create a table using the OrioleDB storage engine just execute the standard `CREATE TABLE` statement. By default it will create a table using OrioleDB storage engine. For example:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create a table\\\\ncreate table blog_post (\\\\n  id int8 not null,\\\\n  title text not null,\\\\n  body text not null,\\\\n  author text not null,\\\\n  published_at timestamptz not null default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\\\\n  views bigint not null,\\\\n  primary key (id)\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating indexes\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB tables always have a primary key. If it wasn't defined explicitly, a hidden primary key is created using the `ctid` column.\\\\nAdditionally you can create secondary indexes.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Currently, only B-tree indexes are supported, so features like pg\\\\\\\\_vector's HNSW indexes are not yet available.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create an index\\\\ncreate index blog_post_published_at on blog_post (published_at);\\\\n\\\\ncreate index blog_post_views on blog_post (views) where (views > 1000);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Data manipulation\\\\n\\\\nYou can query and modify data in OrioleDB tables using standard SQL statements, including `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nINSERT INTO blog_post (id, title, body, author, views)\\\\nVALUES (1, 'Hello, World!', 'This is my first blog post.', 'John Doe', 1000);\\\\n\\\\nSELECT * FROM {"query": "
-- Verify the bug: joining payment (which can have multiple rows per rental)
-- then joining film_actor (which multiplies rows per film) causes overcounting
-- Let's see what customer 1's correct stats should be

-- Correct total_rentals and total_spent for customer 1
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as correct_total_rentals,
    SUM(p.amount) as correct_total_spent,
    AVG(EXTRACT(days FROM (r.return_date - r.rental_date))) as correct_avg_duration
FROM customer c
JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
"}

{"query": "
-- The bug: in customer_basic_stats, joining payment AND inventory causes multiplication
-- because each rental→payment can have MULTIPLE payments, 
-- AND the inventory join is redundant (only needed for film_id, not used in aggregates)
-- Let's see the CORRECT stats, separating payment from rental stats

-- The correct approach:
-- 1. total_rentals = COUNT(DISTINCT rental_id) for rentals with payments
-- 2. total_spent = SUM(payment.amount) for those rentals  
-- 3. avg_rental_duration should be AVG over DISTINCT rentals, not multiplied

-- Test: what's the correct avg_rental_duration for customer 1?
WITH paid_rentals AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT r.rental_id, r.rental_date, r.return_date
    FROM rental r
    INNER JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE r.customer_id = 1
)
SELECT 
    AVG(EXTRACT(days FROM (return_date - rental_date))) as correct_avg_duration
FROM paid_rentals;
"}

-- 1. multiple payments per rental_id → overcounting rentals when joining payment
-- 2. EXTRACT(days) truncates to whole days, should use EPOCH/86400 for fractional days
-- 3. The customer_categories and customer_actors CTEs may also be affected by the actor multiplication

-- Check: does customer_categories have an issue when joining film_actor?
-- In customer_categories, we join payment (ok), but NOT film_actor, so no multiplication from actors
-- BUT: a film can only be in ONE category (confirmed above), so categories CTE should be fine
-- UNLESS: a rental can have multiple payments → that multiplies category_count too!

-- Verify: category count without payment join vs with
SELECT cat.name, COUNT(*) as with_payment_join
FROM customer c
JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id
JOIN category cat ON fc.category_id = cat.category_id
JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1
GROUP BY cat.name
ORDER BY with_payment_join DESC
LIMIT 5;
"}

SELECT r.rental_id, COUNT(p.payment_id) as payment_count
FROM rental r
JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
WHERE r.customer_id = 1
GROUP BY r.rental_id
HAVING COUNT(p.payment_id) > 1;
"}

{"query": "
-- Now I have a clear picture. Let me also understand the regional_popular_films CTE
-- It joins payment, which is correct for filtering to paid rentals only
-- But the email IS NOT NULL filter on customer is also needed (already there)
-- The issue: it also adds WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL which may limit the regional counts
-- to only customers with email. For regional popularity, should we count ALL rentals 
-- in that region or only from customers with emails? The original has this filter, let's keep it consistent.

-- Let me now construct the correct query:
-- ISSUE 1: customer_basic_stats - need to use DISTINCT rental_id for COUNT and duration avg
--   because payment join can create multiple rows per rental
-- ISSUE 2: avg_rental_duration uses EXTRACT(days) which truncates; 
--   should use EXTRACT(epoch)/86400 for accurate fractional days

-- The key fix for customer_basic_stats:
-- Instead of joining payment directly, we should aggregate payment first, then join

-- Test the correct approach for customer_basic_stats:
WITH paid_rental_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        r.rental_id,
        r.customer_id,
        r.inventory_id,
        r.rental_date,
        r.return_date,
        SUM(p.amount) as rental_amount
    FROM rental r
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    GROUP BY r.rental_id, r.customer_id, r.inventory_id, r.rental_date, r.return_date
)
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    COUNT(prs.rental_id) as total_rentals,
    SUM(prs.rental_amount) as total_spent,
    AVG(EXTRACT(epoch FROM (prs.return_date - prs.rental_date))/86400) as avg_rental_duration
FROM customer c
JOIN paid_rental_stats prs ON c.customer_id = prs.customer_id
WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(prs.rental_id) >= 15
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 5;
"}

{"query": "
-- Test the complete fixed query before creating the table
WITH 
-- Pre-aggregate payments per rental to avoid duplication issues
paid_rentals AS (
    SELECT 
        r.rental_id,
        r.customer_id,
        r.inventory_id,
        r.rental_date,
        r.return_date,
        SUM(p.amount) as rental_payment_amount
    FROM rental r
    INNER JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    GROUP BY r.rental_id, r.customer_id, r.inventory_id, r.rental_date, r.return_date
),
customer_basic_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        c.customer_id,
        c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name as customer_name,
        ci.city as customer_city,
        co.country as customer_country,
        COUNT(pr.rental_id) as total_rentals,
        COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id) as unique_films,
        SUM(pr.rental_payment_amount) as total_spent,
        AVG(EXTRACT(epoch FROM (pr.return_date - pr.rental_date))/86400) as avg_rental_duration
    FROM customer c
    JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
    JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
    JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
    JOIN paid_rentals pr ON c.customer_id = pr.customer_id
    JOIN inventory i ON pr.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, ci.city, co.country
    HAVING COUNT(pr.rental_id) >= 15
),
customer_categories AS (
    SELECT 
        c.customer_id,
        cat.name as category_name,
        COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as category_count,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) DESC, cat.name ASC) as rn
    FROM customer c
    JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id
    JOIN category cat ON fc.category_id = cat.category_id
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, cat.name
),
customer_actors AS (
    SELECT 
        c.customer_id,
        a.first_name || ' ' || a.last_name as actor_name,
        COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as actor_count,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) DESC, (a.first_name || ' ' || a.last_name) ASC) as rn
    FROM customer c
    JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    JOIN film_actor fa ON f.film_id = fa.film_id
    JOIN actor a ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, a.first_name, a.last_name
),
regional_popular_films AS (
    SELECT 
        co.country,
        f.title,
        COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as rental_count,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY co.country ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) DESC, f.title ASC) as rn
    FROM rental r
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    JOIN customer c ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
    JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
    JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
    JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY co.country, f.title
)
SELECT 
    cbs.customer_id,
    cbs.customer_name,
    cbs.customer_city,
    cbs.customer_country,
    cbs.total_rentals,
    cbs.unique_films,
    cbs.total_spent,
    cc.category_name as favorite_category,
    ca.actor_name as favorite_actor,
    cbs.avg_rental_duration,
    CASE 
        WHEN cbs.total_spent >= 150 THEN 'Premium'
        WHEN cbs.total_spent >= 75 THEN 'Standard'
        ELSE 'Basic'
    END as customer_tier,
    rpf.title as most_popular_film_in_region,
    rpf.rental_count as regional_film_rental_count
FROM customer_basic_stats cbs
LEFT JOIN customer_categories cc ON cbs.customer_id = cc.customer_id AND cc.rn = 1
LEFT JOIN customer_actors ca ON cbs.customer_id = ca.customer_id AND ca.rn = 1
LEFT JOIN regional_popular_films rpf ON cbs.customer_country = rpf.country AND rpf.rn = 1
ORDER BY cbs.total_spent DESC, cbs.total_rentals DESC, cbs.customer_name ASC
LIMIT 5;
"}

-- Create the customer_analysis_fixed table with corrected query results
CREATE TABLE public.customer_analysis_fixed AS
WITH 
-- Pre-aggregate payments per rental to avoid row duplication from multi-payment rentals
paid_rentals AS (
    SELECT 
        r.rental_id,
        r.customer_id,
        r.inventory_id,
        r.rental_date,
        r.return_date,
        SUM(p.amount) as rental_payment_amount
    FROM rental r
    INNER JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    GROUP BY r.rental_id, r.customer_id, r.inventory_id, r.rental_date, r.return_date
),
customer_basic_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        c.customer_id,
        c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name as customer_name,
        ci.city as customer_city,
        co.country as customer_country,
        COUNT(pr.rental_id) as total_rentals,
        COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id) as unique_films,
        SUM(pr.rental_payment_amount) as total_spent,
        AVG(EXTRACT(epoch FROM (pr.return_date - pr.rental_date))/86400) as avg_rental_duration
    FROM customer c
    JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
    JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
    JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
    JOIN paid_rentals pr ON c.customer_id = pr.customer_id
    JOIN inventory i ON pr.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, ci.city, co.country
    HAVING COUNT(pr.rental_id) >= 15
),
customer_categories AS (
    SELECT 
        c.customer_id,
        cat.name as category_name,
        COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as category_count,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) DESC, cat.name ASC) as rn
    FROM customer c
    JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id
    JOIN category cat ON fc.category_id = cat.category_id
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, cat.name
),
customer_actors AS (
    SELECT 
        c.customer_id,
        a.first_name || ' ' || a.last_name as actor_name,
        COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as actor_count,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) DESC, (a.first_name || ' ' || a.last_name) ASC) as rn
    FROM customer c
    JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    JOIN film_actor fa ON f.film_id = fa.film_id
    JOIN actor a ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, a.first_name, a.last_name
),
regional_popular_films AS (
    SELECT 
        co.country,
        f.title,
        COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) as rental_count,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY co.country ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id) DESC, f.title ASC) as rn
    FROM rental r
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    JOIN customer c ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
    JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
    JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
    JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
    JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
    WHERE c.email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY co.country, f.title
)
SELECT 
    cbs.customer_id,
    cbs.customer_name,
    cbs.customer_city,
    cbs.customer_country,
    cbs.total_rentals,
    cbs.unique_films,
    cbs.total_spent,
    cc.category_name as favorite_category,
    ca.actor_name as favorite_actor,
    cbs.avg_rental_duration,
    CASE 
        WHEN cbs.total_spent >= 150 THEN 'Premium'
        WHEN cbs.total_spent >= 75 THEN 'Standard'
        ELSE 'Basic'
    END as customer_tier,
    rpf.title as most_popular_film_in_region,
    rpf.rental_count as regional_film_rental_count
FROM customer_basic_stats cbs
LEFT JOIN customer_categories cc ON cbs.customer_id = cc.customer_id AND cc.rn = 1
LEFT JOIN customer_actors ca ON cbs.customer_id = ca.customer_id AND ca.rn = 1
LEFT JOIN regional_popular_films rpf ON cbs.customer_country = rpf.country AND rpf.rn = 1
ORDER BY cbs.total_spent DESC, cbs.total_rentals DESC, cbs.customer_name ASC;
"}

The results are perfect. The table has been created successfully with 587 qualifying customers, and the spot-checks confirm the expected values:
- Customer ID 1: `avg_rental_duration = 4.27` ✅ (was 3.90)
- Customer ID 2: `avg_rental_duration = 5.69` ✅ (was 5.23)

---

## Summary of Bugs Found and Fixed

### Bug 1: Row multiplication from multi-payment rentals in `customer_basic_stats`
**Root Cause:** The original query joined `payment` directly to `rental`. Since some rentals have multiple payment records (e.g., rental `4591` had **5** payments), this caused rows to be duplicated. This inflated `total_rentals`, `total_spent`, and distorted `avg_rental_duration`.

**Fix:** Pre-aggregate payments **per rental** in a new `paid_rentals` CTE using `SUM(amount)` and `GROUP BY rental_id` *before* joining to the customer. This ensures each rental is counted exactly once.

### Bug 2: Wrong date extraction function for `avg_rental_duration`
**Root Cause:** `EXTRACT(days FROM interval)` only returns the **integer day component** of an interval (truncating time). For example, a rental of 4 days 6 hours would return `4`, not `4.25`. This caused the reported 3.90 instead of the expected 4.27 for Customer 1.

**Fix:** Changed to `EXTRACT(epoch FROM (return_date - rental_date))/86400`, which converts the full interval to total seconds and divides by seconds-per-day, yielding precise fractional days.

### Bug 3: `COUNT(*)` instead of `COUNT(DISTINCT rental_id)` in `customer_categories` and `customer_actors`
**Root Cause:** Both CTEs used `COUNT(*)` while joining `payment`. Because some rentals had multiple payments, those rentals were counted multiple times per category/actor, skewing the "favorite" ranking.

**Fix:** Changed to `COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id)` in both CTEs so each rental contributes exactly one count regardless of how many payment records it has.

### Bug 4: Same multi-payment issue in `regional_popular_films`
**Root Cause:** `COUNT(*)` was used instead of `COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id)`, meaning films associated with multi-payment rentals appeared more popular than they actually were.

**Fix:** Changed to `COUNT(DISTINCT r.rental_id)` for accurate regional film popularity.
